test_title: PYST 40: SSC CPO - Quantitative Aptitude (Held on 9 Nov 2022 Shift 1)
subject: maths
question: A seller uses faulty weight in place of a 2 kg weight and earns a 25% profit. He claims that he is selling on the cost price in front of the customers but uses a faulty weight. How much error is there in the 2 kg weight to gain 25%?
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Profit = 25% = 1/4

Ratio of Error to True Weight = 1 : 4

Claimed Weight = True Weight + Error = 4 + 1 = 5 units

Given Claimed Weight = 2 kg = 2000 g

⇒ 5 units = 2000 g ⇒ 1 unit (Error) = 400 g

**∴ The correct answer is 400 g.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Claimed weight = 2 kg = 2000 g

Profit earned = 25%

**Formula Used:**

Profit % = [Error ÷ True Weight] × 100

Where, True Weight = Claimed Weight − Error

 
 True Weight (x g)
 
 
 Error
 
 

 Claimed Weight = 2000 g
 
 

 

 Profit = 25%

**Calculations:**

⇒ Let the true weight used by the seller be x grams.

⇒ Error = (2000 − x) g

⇒ Profit % = [(2000 − x) ÷ x] × 100

⇒ 25 = [(2000 − x) ÷ x] × 100

⇒ 25 ÷ 100 = (2000 − x) ÷ x

⇒ 1 ÷ 4 = (2000 − x) ÷ x

⇒ x = 4 × (2000 − x)

⇒ x = 8000 − 4x

⇒ 5x = 8000

⇒ x = 1600 g

⇒ Error = 2000 − 1600 = 400 g

**∴ The correct answer is 400 g.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Dishonest Dealer Concept

When a dealer sells goods at Cost Price but uses a false weight, his profit is purely due to the difference in weight. The formula used is: Profit % = [Error ÷ (Claimed Weight − Error)] × 100.

Double Cheating (Buying and Selling)

If a dishonest dealer cheats by taking more weight while buying and giving less weight while selling, his net profit factor is the product of the multiplying factors at both stages.

Markup and False Weight Combined

If the dealer marks up the price by P% above cost price and uses a false weight, the actual gain involves equating the ratio of the new selling price to cost price along with the false weight ratio.
